answer:
HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, answering "How does age influence the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in?"):

Within this young 1989 NLSY779 cohort (ages 24–32), AGE has at most a weak and non-robust effect on the likelihood of a net savings withdrawal (DISSAVED = 1). Restricting to respondents whose savings actually changed (SAMESAVE = 0 — the only frame in which DISSAVED can equal 1), older AGE is associated with a slightly LOWER probability of DISSAVED = 1, and that decline is concentrated in the transition from the late 20s into the early 30s rather than across the whole range. The raw DISSAVED rate is roughly flat through the mid-20s (~0.50–0.52) and dips to ~0.48 by age 32; a quadratic (inverted-U) logistic fit places the peak around age 27–28.

However, the signal is small and statistically fragile: the linear AGE term is not significant (odds ratio ≈ 0.99 per year, p ≈ 0.39), and the quadratic (AGE_2) term is only nominally significant in the unadjusted model (p ≈ 0.049), becoming non-significant once INCOME, GENDER, BLACK, and HISPANIC are controlled for (p ≈ 0.067) and dropping just above 0.05 when the small age-32 cell is excluded (p ≈ 0.054). The predicted probability of DISSAVED = 1 falls only from ~0.52 near the mid-20s peak to ~0.47 by age 32 (≈ 3 percentage points).

Direction vs. the time-preference story: the observed direction — older age → marginally lower withdrawal propensity — is CONSISTENT with the expectation that time preference moderates toward greater patience with maturity. But the evidence is weak, and DISSAVED is a noisy proxy for time preference: higher INCOME strongly lowers DISSAVED (OR ≈ 0.79, p < 0.0001), so part of the age pattern may reflect the age distribution of income shocks and life-cycle events rather than a true change in patience.

Conservative bottom line: age is weakly, directionally-consistent but not robustly associated with a lower likelihood of withdrawing more than put into savings within this narrow 24–32 window; no strong monotonic or clearly curvilinear age effect can be claimed.

payload.hypothesis: Within the 1989 NLSY79 young cohort (ages 24–32), among respondents whose savings changed (SAMESAVE=0), older AGE is associated with a weakly lower likelihood of withdrawing more than put into savings (DISSAVED=1), with the small decline concentrated from the late 20s into the early 30s (inverted-U peaking ~age 27–28). The effect is directionally consistent with time preference moderating (declining) with maturity but is small and not statistically robust: linear AGE NS (OR≈0.99, p≈0.39); quadratic AGE_2 nominally significant unadjusted (p≈0.049) but NS after adjusting for INCOME, GENDER, BLACK, HISPANIC (p≈0.067).
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded data/nls_bmi_processed.csv (N=12,686); removed 2,151 exact duplicate rows -> N=10,535. 2) Verified structural gate SAMESAVE=1 => DISSAVED=0; adopted SAMESAVE=0 (N=5,821) as the primary analytical frame. 3) Descriptive table of DISSAVED rate by single-year AGE. 4) Fit logistic regressions with AGE centered at its mean: (a) linear DISSAVED~AGE_c; (b) quadratic DISSAVED~AGE_c+AGE_c2; compared via likelihood-ratio test and Wald test, plus HC3 robust SEs. 5) Covariate-adjusted model adding log(INCOME), GENDER, BLACK, HISPANIC. 6) Full-sample model for comparison. 7) Sensitivity: excluded the small age-32 cell. 8) Computed predicted probabilities, the quadratic vertex, and the marginal effect of age at the mean. All modeling in analysis.py (statsmodels).
